title: LLM Evaluation
interviewAnswer: Define task-specific datasets and success criteria, then combine deterministic checks, model-based judges where appropriate, and human review. Track quality, latency, cost and safety together.
why: LLM systems are stochastic and task-dependent, so “it looked good in a few prompts” is not an engineering evaluation strategy.
intuition: Turn the application goal into measurable dimensions: correctness, groundedness, usefulness, safety, latency and cost. Build a stable test set and compare changes against it.
deepDive: Use exact/programmatic checks where possible, model-based judges for subjective dimensions, and human review for calibration/high-risk cases. Evaluate components separately: retrieval, tool selection, structured output, final response. Include adversarial and edge cases. Report distributions and failure categories rather than one aggregate score. Version prompts, models and datasets so regressions are reproducible.
workedExample: For a tool-using planning assistant, evaluate whether it chooses the correct function and arguments, whether the numerical result matches the tool output, whether the explanation is useful, and total latency/cost.
commonMistakes: Using only BLEU/ROUGE for open-ended assistant quality.
Changing the test set every time a model changes.
Trusting one LLM judge without human calibration or pairwise consistency checks.
followUps: How would you build an eval set?
production: Run evals in CI before prompt/model releases and online monitoring after deployment. Keep failure traces so qualitative regressions can be diagnosed, not just counted.
